text:
TRICARE 2027 costs are posted: retiree Prime is $396 or $480 a year, Young Adult Prime is $893 a month, and pharmacy copays stay frozen. Every 2027 table.

Editor, FedTools · Editor of FedTools. U.S. federal employee with 20+ years of federal experience, publishing under a pen name to keep outside writing cleanly separated from official duties. Full bio →

By the FedTools editorial team · Reviewed by Jonathan D., 20-year federal employee · Updated November 2026

Last Updated: November 7, 2026 Reading Time: 7 min

TRICARE 2027 costs are now posted on tricare.mil, two days before open season opens on November 9. Retiree enrollment fees rise about 3.7%, TRICARE Young Adult Prime jumps 12.5% to $893 a month, and pharmacy copays stay at 2026 rates. Here is every 2027 fee, deductible, cap and premium next to its 2026 figure.

Which TRICARE 2027 Costs Apply to You: Group A or Group B

Your costs depend on your beneficiary category and your group. Both are set by when the sponsor first joined.

Group A: the sponsor's initial enlistment or appointment began before January 1, 2018.

Group B: it began on or after January 1, 2018.

The premium plans (TRICARE Reserve Select, TRICARE Retired Reserve and TRICARE Young Adult) follow Group B cost rules for deductibles and copays, whatever the sponsor's group. Only their premiums are set separately.

TRICARE 2027 Enrollment Fees for Retirees

These are annual fees for retirees, their families, survivors and others.

Plan 2026 2027 Change Prime, Group A, individual $381.96 $396.00 +$14.04 (+3.7%) Prime, Group A, family $765.00 $792.96 +$27.96 (+3.7%) Select, Group A, individual $186.96 $193.92 +$6.96 (+3.7%) Select, Group A, family $375.00 $388.92 +$13.92 (+3.7%) Prime, Group B, individual $462.96 $480.00 +$17.04 (+3.7%) Prime, Group B, family $927.00 $960.00 +$33.00 (+3.6%) Select, Group B, individual $594.96 $616.92 +$21.96 (+3.7%) Select, Group B, family $1,191.00 $1,233.96 +$42.96 (+3.6%)

Sources: tricare.mil Health Plan Costs (calendar year 2027), TRICARE Newsroom 2026 cost tables. Percent change computed by FedTools from the unrounded fees.

The TRICARE page lists two exceptions:

The Prime Group A fee is waived if you are under 65 and have Medicare Part A and Part B.

Select Group A is $0 for medically retired sponsors, their families and survivors.

The Group B premium over Group A is now $84 a year for an individual on Prime and $423 a year on Select. A Group B retiree family on Select pays $845.04 more than a Group A family for the same plan.

Retiree Deductibles and Catastrophic Caps for 2027

Prime has no deductible. Select does, and the Group B deductible rises again.

Item 2026 2027 Select Group A deductible $150 individual / $300 family $150 / $300 (no change) Select Group B deductible, network $198 / $397 $205 / $411 Select Group B deductible, non-network $397 / $794 $411 / $823 Catastrophic cap, Prime Group A $3,000 $3,000 (no change) Catastrophic cap, Select Group A $4,381 $4,538 Catastrophic cap, Group B (Prime and Select) $4,635 $4,802

The catastrophic cap is the yearly limit on what a family pays out of pocket for covered services. Select Group A keeps a $3,000 cap for medically retired sponsors, their families and survivors.

Retiree Copays: The Visits You Pay For

Most network copays rise by a dollar to five dollars. The table covers the visits retirees use most.

Network visit Prime (A and B) Select Group A Select Group B Primary care $26 → $27 $38 → $40 $33 → $34 Specialty care $39 → $41 $52 → $52 $52 → $54 Urgent care $39 → $41 $38 → $40 $52 → $54 Emergency room $79 → $82 $138 → $143 $105 → $109

Prime inpatient admissions go from $198 to $205 per admission. Select Group B inpatient admissions go from $231 to $240. Preventive care stays $0 in every plan.

Active Duty Family Members: Group A Unchanged

Active duty service members pay nothing. Family members on Prime still pay $0 in enrollment fees and deductibles.

On Select, Group A family members see no change for 2027: a $50 / $100 deductible for sponsors in E-1 to E-4, $150 / $300 for E-5 and above, and a $1,000 catastrophic cap.

Group B family members on Select pay a little more:

Group B, Select 2026 2027 Deductible, E-1 to E-4 $66 individual / $132 family $68 / $137 Deductible, E-5 and above $198 / $397 $205 / $411 Catastrophic cap (Prime and Select) $1,324 $1,372

TRICARE Young Adult Premiums 2027: The Biggest Jump

The premium plans rose the most. These are monthly premiums.

Premium plan 2026 2027 Change TRICARE Young Adult-Prime $794.00 $893.00 +$99.00 (+12.5%) TRICARE Young Adult-Select $363.00 $394.00 +$31.00 (+8.5%) TRICARE Retired Reserve, member only $645.90 $707.59 +$61.69 (+9.6%) TRICARE Retired Reserve, member and family $1,548.30 $1,697.70 +$149.40 (+9.6%) TRICARE Reserve Select, member only $57.88 $60.54 +$2.66 (+4.6%) TRICARE Reserve Select, member and family $286.66 $307.48 +$20.82 (+7.3%)

Sources: tricare.mil Health Plan Costs (calendar year 2027), TRICARE Newsroom 2026 Table 5. Annual figures are the monthly premium x 12.

Over a full year, TRICARE Young Adult-Prime costs $10,716 in 2027 and Young Adult-Select costs $4,728. That gap is $5,988 a year for the same young adult.

TYA covers adult children who have aged out of regular TRICARE and are under 26. Deductibles and caps follow the sponsor's status:

Active duty or Reserve Select sponsor: Young Adult-Select deductible is $68 for E-1 to E-4 and $205 for E-5 and above, with a $1,372 cap.

Retired or Retired Reserve sponsor: Young Adult-Select deductible is $205 network and $411 non-network, with a $4,802 cap.

If your adult child is healthy and lives near network doctors, Select at $394 a month is the cheaper door. Prime makes sense mainly when the child needs regular specialty care and lives inside a Prime service area. Compare it against the child's own job-based plan, or a parent's FEHB Self and Family plan if you are also a federal employee.

TRICARE Retired Reserve covers gray-area reservists until 60. Our TRICARE Retired Reserve cost breakdown walks through the 2026 math against civilian plans; at $1,697.70 a month, family coverage now runs $20,372.40 for 2027.

What Is Not Going Up in 2027

Pharmacy copays are frozen. DHA's calendar year 2027 notice in the Federal Register (91 FR 59115, September 18, 2026) keeps 2026 rates: $16 generic, $48 brand-name and $85 non-formulary for a 30-day retail network fill, and $14, $44 and $85 for a 90-day mail-order fill.

Active duty family members in Group A also see no change in fees, deductibles or caps from 2026.

What to Do Before Open Season Closes December 8

Open season runs November 9 to December 8, 2026. It covers TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select. Any change you make takes effect January 1, 2027.

Find your group. Check your sponsor's first enlistment or appointment date against January 1, 2018.

Add up a year. Take the 2027 enrollment fee, then add the copays for the visits you actually expect. Prime costs more up front; Select costs more per visit.

Check the Young Adult choice separately. Open season covers Prime and Select only; it does not apply to TRICARE Young Adult, Reserve Select or Retired Reserve, which follow their own purchase rules. TYA-Prime costs $5,988 more a year than TYA-Select in 2027, so compare the two at the new prices.

Read the switch rules. Our TRICARE Open Season 2027 guide covers the dates, the Prime-to-Select mechanics and what happens if you miss the window.

Compare TRICARE With FEHB

If you are a military retiree working for the federal government, you can carry TRICARE, FEHB or both. Use the free TRICARE vs FEHB Calculator to compare your 2027 TRICARE fee against an FEHB premium for your enrollment type.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is TRICARE Prime for retirees in 2027?

TRICARE Prime costs $396 a year for an individual and $792.96 for a family in Group A. In Group B it costs $480 and $960. The Group A fee is waived if you are under 65 and have Medicare Part A and Part B.

How much is TRICARE Young Adult in 2027?

TRICARE Young Adult-Prime is $893 a month in 2027, up from $794. TRICARE Young Adult-Select is $394 a month, up from $363. That is $10,716 and $4,728 a year.

Did TRICARE pharmacy copays go up for 2027?

No. The 2027 program notice froze pharmacy copays at 2026 rates: $16 generic, $48 brand-name and $85 non-formulary for a 30-day retail network fill, and $14, $44 and $85 for 90-day mail order.

When can I change my TRICARE plan for 2027?

For TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select, during open season, November 9 to December 8, 2026. Changes take effect January 1, 2027. Outside open season you need a qualifying life event. Open season does not apply to TRICARE Young Adult, Reserve Select or Retired Reserve.

How do I know if I am in TRICARE Group A or Group B?

It depends on the sponsor's first enlistment or appointment. Before January 1, 2018 is Group A. On or after that date is Group B.

text:
Leidos Holdings, a Reston, Virginia-based defense technology and government services company, reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $4.63 billion, representing a 4% increase from the prior-year period. The company also generated $413 million in net income, secured $5.5 billion in new bookings, and increased its full-year adjusted earnings guidance as demand for defense technology, intelligence, cybersecurity, and air traffic management solutions remained strong.

Revenue increased from $4.47 billion in the third quarter of 2025, supported by higher demand for defense technology products, air traffic management solutions, and intelligence mission support.

The acquisition of ENTRUST Solutions also contributed to growth, partially offsetting declines in certain managed healthcare and federal civilian information technology programs.

Net income increased 12% year-over-year to $413 million from $369 million.

GAAP diluted earnings per share increased 16% to $3.28 from $2.82, while net income margin improved to 8.9% from 8.3%.

On a non-GAAP basis, diluted earnings per share increased 19% to $3.62 from $3.05.

Adjusted EBITDA reached $644 million, representing a 5% increase from $616 million in the prior-year period. Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded slightly to 13.9%.

Leidos generated $523 million in cash flow from operating activities and $476 million in free cash flow during the quarter.

The company also returned $556 million to shareholders, including $504 million in share repurchases and $52 million through its quarterly dividend program.

Its board subsequently declared a quarterly dividend of $0.45 per share, representing a 4.7% increase from the previous quarter.

One of the most significant developments was Leidos’ continued growth in government contracts.

The company reported $5.5 billion in third-quarter net bookings, representing a book-to-bill ratio of 1.2.

Total backlog reached $49.6 billion at quarter-end, including $11.1 billion in funded backlog. Total and funded backlog increased 4% and 22% year-over-year, respectively.

New awards included a $717 million contract supporting the U.S. Air Force Air Combat Command’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance operations.

Under the agreement, Leidos will provide intelligence mission support and advanced data integration across 35 locations worldwide.

The company also received a $672 million Transportation Security Administration contract to deploy, relocate, and manage security screening equipment at federalized U.S. airports and major domestic special events.

Another major award involved a $318 million sole-source bridge contract supporting the Defense Health Agency’s MHS GENESIS electronic health record system.

The agreement covers system maintenance, cybersecurity, performance monitoring, technology updates, and user support.

Leidos secured a $301 million U.S. Army contract to provide continuous defensive cyber operations.

The work includes deployment of the company’s UpHold Effect Agentic SOC Automation platform, which uses autonomous AI agents to support cybersecurity monitoring and response.

In space and missile defense, Leidos received a $272 million award from Sierra Space to provide infrared sensing payloads, onboard signal processing, and mission support for 18 missile-tracking satellites.

The company also won a $170 million contract to modernize flight data processing software for the United Kingdom’s National Air Traffic Services.

Additional awards included a $160 million U.S. Cyber Command support contract, a $155 million U.S. Navy contract involving sea-launched cruise missile development, and a $129 million electronic health record agreement supporting U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Leidos also secured separate radar-related awards of $95 million and $41 million for the U.S. Army and Marine Corps, respectively.

The company received a $27 million U.S. Special Operations Command contract for initial production of its AGM-190A Havoc Spear small cruise missile.

These awards expand Leidos’ role across national security, defense modernization, intelligence systems, cybersecurity, and government technology services.

Leidos also completed a transaction with Altaris on October 5, 2026, contributing its Security Enterprise Solutions and Industrial Automation businesses to a newly established joint venture.

Following that transaction and its third-quarter performance, Leidos updated its full-year 2026 outlook.

The company expects revenue between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, compared with its previous projection of $18.2 billion to $18.4 billion, reflecting the portfolio changes.

Its adjusted EBITDA margin outlook remains in the mid-13% range.

Leidos increased its non-GAAP diluted earnings per share forecast to between $12.50 and $12.70, compared with its previous range of $12.20 to $12.50.

The updated guidance represents the company’s third consecutive quarterly improvement to its full-year earnings outlook.

Leidos continues pursuing its NorthStar 2030 strategy, emphasizing technology differentiation, operational performance, strategic investment, and disciplined capital allocation.

The company’s financial performance and contract backlog illustrate its established role in supporting defense and government modernization programs while providing a foundation for future revenue opportunities.

KEY QUOTES

“Leidos delivered another quarter of strong financial performance, allowing us to enhance our 2026 guidance for the third consecutive quarter. Our sustained momentum reflects the strength of our focused team, united behind our NorthStar 2030 strategy and committed to delivering on our customers’ most critical missions. Looking ahead, we’ll continue to execute our strategy with confidence, invest in differentiated capabilities, and deploy capital strategically to accelerate growth and create enduring value.”

title: TRICARE costs remain mostly stable in 2027, but some premiums spike
description:
Military-sponsored health insurance costs will remain stable for most troops and their families in 2027, with some slight increases in copays and out-of-pocket cost caps.
“Each TRICARE plan has distinct features that beneficiaries should consider,” Valerie Palmer, a TRICARE management and program analyst at the Defense Health Agency, said in a release last month.

text:
Military-sponsored health insurance costs will remain stable for most troops and their families in 2027, with some slight increases in copays and out-of-pocket cost caps.

The Defense Department released the prices of next year’s coverage options Thursday ahead of TRICARE’s open enrollment season, which runs Nov. 9-Dec. 8. Service members and dependents can keep the plan they already have or switch to one that better meets their needs.

Though the two main TRICARE plans, Prime and Select, won’t see significant changes in 2027, double-digit premium spikes in some of the unsubsidized options worry military family advocates the monthly price will drive away enrollees or overly strain their wallets.

“Each TRICARE plan has distinct features that beneficiaries should consider,” Valerie Palmer, a TRICARE management and program analyst at the Defense Health Agency, said in a release last month. “Your preferred providers, expected health care costs and rules around referrals or pre-authorizations may all play a role in choosing a plan.”

TRICARE Prime

Government subsidies make TRICARE more affordable and less volatile than coverage offered through private employers, the Affordable Care Act marketplaces and commercial insurers themselves. The program serves around 9.4 million service members, retirees and their families worldwide.

Whether officer or enlisted, active-duty service members are automatically enrolled in TRICARE Prime and do not pay monthly premiums or for the care they receive. Their dependents also are not charged an enrollment fee or, in most cases, a premium to continue their insurance.

In 2027, Prime continues to offer premium-free coverage in exchange for picking a provider to manage a person’s care and write specialist referrals. Family members of active-duty troops who joined before 2018 — known as Group A — must cover the first $1,000 of their medical costs before insurance kicks in to cover the rest. If the planholder joined the military in 2018 or later — known as Group B — that cap is set at $1,372.

There are no copays for care if a patient follows their plan’s rules, like seeing a provider in the TRICARE network and obtaining referrals as needed. Charges also apply when picking up a prescription outside of a military pharmacy.

TRICARE Select

TRICARE Select offers more flexibility to see providers without a referral, but for a higher price. Though active-duty troops and their families aren’t charged to enroll in a plan, they must hit a deductible ranging between $50 and $411 per year, depending on their grade and time in service, before the Defense Department begins to cover their care.

The military’s newest families will see deductible increases of less than 4%, depending on their sponsor’s grade, if they opt into TRICARE Select. Deductibles won’t change for dependents of troops who joined before 2018.

Select members must also foot the bill for copays until they reach their annual cap. Like Prime, that limit sits at $1,000 for Group A families and $1,372 for Group B families. Patients are charged a flat copay for each visit to an in-network provider, or 20% of the total cost for non-network providers. Those fees will rise by a few dollars apiece, depending on the services sought, next year.

Causes for concern

Premiums for a Young Adult Prime plan are set to spike more than 12% to nearly $900 per month — around $10,700 per year for dependents between ages 21-26. Retired Reserve family plan premiums will hit nearly $1,700 per month — or $20,400 per year — almost 10% more than the previous year.

A DHA spokesperson said TYA Prime has a “relatively small” number of members who frequently seek care, driving up premiums to cover the government’s cost of those services. Nearly 1,300 young adults were enrolled in Prime as of September, compared to more than 27,600 in Select.

Military family advocates have pushed for Congress to subsidize TRICARE’s premium-based plans to relieve that financial burden, particularly for those in their early 20s who are less likely to have the income or savings to cover high insurance costs.

Humana Military and TriWest Healthcare Alliance are entering their third year of ensuring the insurance program’s underlying systems run smoothly. The firms won a pair of managed care support contracts totaling $136 billion in 2022, but have had a rocky start marred by customer woes like lost referrals and unpaid medical bills.

Lawmakers have also recently questioned whether the pharmacy benefit manager Express Scripts is pushing patients to receive more medications through its mail-order branch, rather than in person, to boost its own revenue. DoD has said giving Express Scripts more latitude over the pharmacy process has helped save money.

Pharmacy costs won’t change next year, regardless of plan, DHA said.

title: TRICARE 2027 Costs: Fees, Deductibles, Caps, Premiums - Military Toolkit
description: TRICARE published CY2027 costs Nov 5, 2026: Group B family cap $1,372.00, retiree Select Group B fee $1,233.96, TRS family $307.48 a month. Each change vs 2026.
text:
The bottom line up front

On November 5, 2026 , the TRICARE Newsroom published "Get to know your 2027 TRICARE health plan costs," and tricare.mil's cost comparison page was updated the same day to read "for 2027, unless noted." That completes the price list the September 18 Federal Register notice left open: every enrollment fee, deductible, copayment, catastrophic cap and monthly premium for calendar year 2027 is printed in five tables, effective January 1, 2027 . Open season runs November 9 through December 8, 2026 . Two things are still not out: the TRICARE For Life 2027 cost matrix, which "will be posted early next year," and any 2027 figure for the Continued Health Care Benefit Program, which the 2026 article carried in a sixth table and this one does not.

What these figures are and are not

Every TRICARE figure below is the Defense Health Agency's published calendar year 2027 amount as printed on November 5, 2026, compared with the amount it printed for 2026. The pay figures are 2026 basic pay from the DFAS table effective January 1, 2026, because the 2027 pay table is not final. Always verify with your finance office and the TRICARE cost comparison page before making financial decisions.

Active duty service members still pay nothing. Their families on TRICARE Prime still pay no enrollment fee, no deductible and no copayments as long as they follow the referral rules. On TRICARE Select the picture splits by group: Group A, a sponsor whose initial enlistment or appointment began before January 1, 2018, keeps the deductibles and the $1,000.00 cap that 10 U.S.C. 1079 writes as fixed dollar amounts; Group B, on or after that date, has indexed figures that moved.

Active duty family on TRICARE Select

One Group A line went down: the network copayment for an outpatient ground ambulance is $86.00 in 2027 against $88.00 in 2026. The article's own note says costs change "based on the law, the federal cost of living adjustment, and the costs of healthcare services and prescription drugs," and the ambulance figure follows the cost of the service, not the COLA. The catastrophic cap counts deductibles and enrollment fees but not premiums, so $1,372.00 is the most a Group B family pays for covered care in 2027.

Retired sponsors and their families pay the enrollment fees, and the family fee is where the dollars are. Every 2027 fee divides evenly by twelve, to the cent, which is why the Select figures end in odd cents: $1,233.96 is $102.83 a month.

Retiree enrollment fee or cap

Retiree copayments moved by a dollar or a few. Prime primary care is $27.00 (was $26.00), specialty $41.00 (was $39.00) and an emergency room visit $82.00 (was $79.00), the same in both groups. Select Group A network primary care is $40.00 (was $38.00) and the emergency room $143.00 (was $138.00); Select Group B is $34.00, $54.00 and $109.00 (was $33.00, $52.00 and $105.00). One exception sits in a note: the Select Group A cap for survivors of active duty deaths and for medically retired members and their families stays at $3,000.00, the carve-out in 10 U.S.C. 1075(e)(3).

The indexing is in the statute. 10 U.S.C. 1075(d)(2) says each fixed dollar amount in the TRICARE Select table, and the retiree enrollment fee and cap in subsection (e), "shall be annually indexed to the amount by which retired pay is increased under section 1401a of this title, rounded to the next lower multiple of $1," with the leftover cents "carried over to, and accumulated with" later years. 10 U.S.C. 1075a(b)(2) does the same for TRICARE Prime. The retired pay increase under section 1401a for December 2026 is 3.6 percent , from the third-quarter CPI-W, which we worked through when the September index was released . The published figures land where that arithmetic points: $4,635.00 times 1.036 is $4,801.86 and DHA printed $4,802.00; $1,324.00 times 1.036 is $1,371.66 and DHA printed $1,372.00. The dollar of difference on some lines is the carry-over clause at work.

TRICARE Reserve Select and TRICARE Retired Reserve are not indexed to retired pay. 10 U.S.C. 1076d(d)(3)(A) sets the TRS premium at "28 percent of the total monthly amount determined on an appropriate actuarial basis," and 10 U.S.C. 1076e(d)(3) sets the TRR premium at "the cost of coverage that the Secretary determines on an appropriate actuarial basis." Both follow the cost of care, so both rose faster than 3.6 percent.

Monthly premium

A Guard or Reserve family on TRS pays $3,689.76 for the year in 2027; a gray-area retiree family on TRR pays $20,372.40. The Young Adult figures match the TRICARE Operations Manual ( priced against a sponsor's basic pay here ). All three premium plans follow TRICARE Select Group B deductibles and copayments regardless of when the sponsor joined. Drilling members can set the TRS premium against a weekend in the drill pay calculator .

TRICARE prices are flat and basic pay is not. The rows below are an active duty family on TRICARE Select in Group B, which now covers most of the force, with 2026 basic pay from our own DFAS table. The deductible splits at E-4, the only place rank touches a TRICARE price directly.

Grade and years of service

A bad medical year now costs an E-3 family 3.79 percent of basic pay and an O-5 family 1.00 percent, against 3.66 and 0.97 on the 2026 cap. The 2027 pay raise, once enacted, will pull those shares back down a little; the basic pay tables carry the current rate for every grade and the RMC calculator shows where health care sits inside total compensation.

No single table fits every retiree, so the rows below use a stand-in anyone can reproduce from our data: 50 percent of 2026 basic pay at the years shown, the multiplier a 20-year legacy High-3 retirement earns, before the December 2026 COLA. A real High-3 average is a little lower than final basic pay and the 3.6 percent adjustment lifts the 2027 payments, so the shares are approximate. The High-3 calculator runs your own numbers.

Grade and years at retirement

For a retired E-6 family in Group B, the Select enrollment fee alone is 3.9 percent of retired pay before a single visit, and a year that reaches the cap takes more than 15 percent. The same fee is 1.35 percent for a retired O-6. Group A retirees pay less than half: $388.92 for Select and $792.96 for Prime. A retirement budget built on the final pay or High-3 estimate should be read net of that fee.

Worked example

Worked example: the same year of care, 2026 and 2027, for two Group B families on TRICARE Select

The deductible is counted in full because the eleven visits exceed it. The retired family's $2,133.96 is 5.7 percent of the E-7 over 20 stand-in retired pay of $37,474.20 and is still well under the $4,802.00 cap. Published CY2026 and CY2027 network copayments from the two TRICARE Newsroom articles; the pattern of care is ours.

Pay figures are FY2026 basic pay from the DFAS table effective January 1, 2026, and TRICARE figures are the Defense Health Agency's published CY2027 amounts as of November 5, 2026. Always verify with your finance office before making financial decisions.

Sources

Figures reflect 2026 rates and regulations. This guide is general information, not personalized financial or tax advice. Always verify with your finance office or a tax professional before making a decision. How we research and source: our methodology .

FAQ

Keep reading

Pay & Allowances

TRICARE Published Half of Its 2027 Price List: Drug Copays Are Frozen by Law, the Rest Waits on the COLA

The Defense Health Agency published the CY2027 TRICARE program changes on September 18, 2026. Pharmacy copayments do not move on January 1, because a statute fixes them through 2027. Enrollment fees, deductibles and catastrophic caps are missing from the notice entirely, because they ride on a cost of living adjustment nobody can compute until October 14. Here is what is settled, what is not, and what the published 2026 figures are worth by rank.

Family & Spouse

TRICARE Young Adult Premiums for 2027: $394 a Month for Select, $893 for Prime, Priced Against Your Basic Pay

The TRICARE Operations Manual now prints the 2027 TRICARE Young Adult premiums: $394.00 a month for Select and $893.00 for Prime, starting January 1, 2027. That is $4,728.00 and $10,716.00 a year for each adult child, with no family rate. Here is what that means against a sponsor's basic pay, and the rules that cost families money when they miss them.

Retirement & Transition

The 2027 COLA Is 3.6%: September CPI-W Closes the Formula for Retired Pay, SBP and VA Compensation

BLS published the September Consumer Price Index on October 14, 2026, the last of the three months that set next year's cost of living adjustment for military retired pay, SBP annuities and VA compensation. The arithmetic is now closed: the 2027 COLA is 3.6%, and Social Security announced the same figure the same morning. Here is the calculation, what it is worth by retired grade, and the one piece still missing on the VA side.

Retirement & Transition

TRICARE For Life at 65: You Must Take Medicare Part B to Keep TRICARE, What It Costs in 2026, and the Sign-Up Window TRICARE Sets

TRICARE For Life has no enrollment form and no enrollment fee, but it only exists once you hold Medicare Part A and Part B. Skip Part B at 65 and TRICARE ends, except for prescriptions at a military pharmacy. Here is the rule in the statute, the 2026 Part B premium by income, the penalty for signing up late, and the sign-up window TRICARE's own brochure gives.

description:
Military families facing flood conditions across North Georgia can now get emergency prescription refills through Nov. 15, defense officials announced Thursday.
The relief protocol runs through Nov. 15 to ensure residents do not lose access to essential medications while floodwaters threaten local communities.
Beneficiaries who need an emergency supply should bring their medication bottle directly to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy.
If the bottle was destroyed or washed away in the flooding, patients can call Express Scripts, Inc. at 1-877-363-1303 or ask a local retail network pharmacist for help.

text:
Military families facing flood conditions across North Georgia can now get emergency prescription refills through Nov. 15, defense officials announced Thursday.

What we know:

The Defense Health Agency authorized the temporary medication waivers for beneficiaries living in Fannin, Gilmer, Murray and Union counties.

The relief protocol runs through Nov. 15 to ensure residents do not lose access to essential medications while floodwaters threaten local communities.

Beneficiaries who need an emergency supply should bring their medication bottle directly to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy.

If the bottle was destroyed or washed away in the flooding, patients can call Express Scripts, Inc. at 1-877-363-1303 or ask a local retail network pharmacist for help.

What you can do:

Patients should visit the original pharmacy where the prescription was filled whenever possible, according to health officials.

If a retail chain filled the medicine, any sister store in that chain can dispense the refill.

Doctors can also phone in brand-new orders to any network location if patients reach them, officials noted.

Beneficiaries can look up active open locations through the online Express Scripts network pharmacy locator or check the Express Scripts weather notices page for storm updates.

All beneficiaries other than active duty service members can visit any authorized urgent care center or doctor without a referral if their normal doctor cannot practice because of the storm.

Anyone experiencing a life-threatening medical emergency should call 911 or visit the closest emergency room immediately.

What we don't know:

Defense officials did not announce whether the temporary waiver will be extended past Nov. 15 if local floodwaters continue to rise.

Emergency authorities have not yet released estimates on the total number of damaged medical facilities across North Georgia.

title: TRICARE Timely Filing Limit: East, West and the Exceptions
description:
TRICARE timely filing at a glance Every row has a source below.
The proof of timely filing guide covers what counts as proof, and the CO-29 guide covers how a timely filing denial shows up on a remittance.
Humana Military, Claims, TRICARE East provider page.
TriWest, TRICARE claims instructions.
TriWest, Timely filing waivers.
text:
A TRICARE claim has one year. That’s the rule in both regions, East and West, and it comes from TRICARE’s own operations manual. A claim filed more than a year after the care is denied unless one of five exceptions applies.

Where the year starts depends on what you bill. The exceptions are narrower than they sound, too. The one for other insurance only helps when that insurer decided the claim after your year had already run out.

This guide gives the rules from the manual, from tricare.mil and from the two regional contractors, Humana Military in the East and TriWest in the West, rechecked on November 6, 2026.

TRICARE timely filing at a glance

Every row has a source below. The row people get wrong is other insurance, so it has its own section.

East or West: who gets the claim

TRICARE runs on regional contracts. On January 1, 2025, TriWest Healthcare Alliance took over the West Region, and Humana Military kept the East.

TriWest lists 26 states in the West: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Six of those moved from the East that day: Arkansas, Illinois, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Texas and Wisconsin. Humana Military runs the East Region. Near a region line, check the patient’s ZIP code with the region tool on tricare.mil.

PGBA processes the claims in both regions. In the East it replaced WPS on January 1, 2025. Humana Military’s claims page adds one condition for the East: “All claims must be submitted electronically in order to receive payment for services.”

One year, and where it starts

TRICARE’s manual puts the rule in one line. The contractor processes claims “filed no later than one year after the date the services were provided.”

For a hospital’s inpatient facility charges, the year runs from the date of discharge. Professional claims for care during the stay still run from each date of service. A claim that misses its year is denied unless one of the exceptions below applies.

The year counts by the calendar. The manual’s own example gives a March 22, 2022 date of service until March 22, 2023.

TriWest recommends filing within 30 days of the date of service anyway. For patients who live overseas, tricare.mil gives 3 years from the date of service or discharge.

One visit, counted

Take an office visit on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, and a remittance dated Thursday, December 3, 2026:

The facility deadline lands on a Saturday. Don’t count on an extra day for the weekend. File by Friday, November 19.

The last row only works if the claim went to the other insurer before November 10, 2027. The next two sections explain why.

The five exceptions

TRICARE’s manual lists five ways a late claim can still be processed. Each one needs proof, and each is narrower than its name.

Retroactive eligibility or authorization. The patient’s eligibility, or an authorization, was granted after the year had run out. If it came through inside the year, the normal year still applies. A bill alone isn’t accepted as proof the care happened.

Administrative error. A mistake or misrepresentation by someone at TRICARE or a contractor kept you from filing on time. You need a statement and the records that show it.

Mental incompetency. The patient was mentally incompetent, which includes being unable to communicate because of a physical disability, and had no legal guardian. A physician’s statement goes with each claim.

Other insurance. The claim went to the other insurer in time, and that insurer decided it after the TRICARE year ran out. You then get 90 calendar days from its decision.

Medicare. For a patient with both, if Medicare accepted the claim as timely, TRICARE processes it when it arrives within 90 calendar days of Medicare’s decision.

The manual looks back six years at most. It only considers services received in the six years before the request.

Waiver requests go to the contractor for your region, with the proof attached. In the West, TriWest takes them at TRICARE West Correspondence, P.O. Box 2748, Virginia Beach, VA 23450.

Other insurance: the year keeps running

TRICARE pays after other health insurance, with a few exceptions such as Medicaid and TRICARE supplements. TriWest is blunt about the order. If TRICARE receives the claim before the other plan processes it, the claim is denied. Paper claims need the other plan’s EOB, and electronic claims need the coordination of benefits data.

Waiting on the other plan doesn’t stop TRICARE’s clock. The year still runs from the date of service. The manual grants an exception only when the claim went to the other insurer before the TRICARE deadline and that insurer’s decision came after it.

Then the claim has to reach TRICARE within 90 calendar days of the other plan’s decision. Send a statement with the date you first billed the other plan and the date it decided, plus its EOB.

So if the other plan answers while your year is still running, file inside the year. Don’t count on the 90 days.

Corrected claims

TriWest’s claim rules for the West give corrections no deadline of their own, so keep them inside the year. A corrected claim replaces the original completely, so send every line, not just the one you fixed.

On an 837, put frequency code 7 in CLM05-3, F8 in REF01 and the original claim number in REF02. Use 8 to void a claim. On paper, the code goes in box 22 of the CMS-1500 with the original claim number, or in the third digit of the UB-04 bill type with the claim number in box 64.

Don’t resend a claim that still shows as in process. TriWest asks providers not to.

Humana Military’s claims page gives East corrections no deadline either. For a reject or denial from its claims auditing, it asks for a corrected claim with supporting documentation, one claim at a time.

Reconsiderations and appeals: 90 days

Both regions give 90 days to dispute a processed claim. Which door you use depends on the denial, and on whether you’re in the network.

In the West, TriWest takes a claim reconsideration “no later than 90 days from the date of the remittance.” It covers allowed amounts, other insurance, timely filing denials, penalties for missing authorization, and denial codes.

A formal appeal is for a different kind of denial: a TRICARE policy limit, care found not medically necessary, or a point of service charge when the care was an emergency. TriWest needs it “within 90 days of the date on the remittance advice.”

Network providers can’t file those appeals. TRICARE’s manual says it plainly: “A network provider is never a proper appealing party.” A provider outside the network can appeal only as a participating provider on that claim.

TRICARE’s manual sets the same 90 calendar days for both regions, counted from the date of the initial denial notice, and the East Region’s appeals page on tricare.mil gives 90 days from the denial date. The manual counts the day after the decision as day one.

Service members: no deadline

Civilian care for active duty service members is paid through the Supplemental Health Care Program. TRICARE’s manual tells contractors not to apply the claims filing deadline to any eligible service member’s claim under that program, or to family member claims under it.

TRICARE For Life: Medicare goes first

For patients with Medicare and TRICARE For Life, you bill Medicare. Medicare pays its share and sends the claim on to WPS Government Services, the TFL contractor, for TRICARE’s part.

The same one year applies in the U.S. And when Medicare accepted a claim as timely, TRICARE’s manual treats it as timely too, as long as it arrives within 90 calendar days of Medicare’s decision.

Turn it into dates

Our timely filing calculator has TRICARE built in. Open it with TRICARE chosen, enter the date of service, and it gives the one year deadline and flags one that lands on a weekend or a holiday.

If you also see Veterans through community care, our VA community care timely filing guide covers that program’s 180 days. Timely filing limits by payer sets out Medicare and the commercial payers side by side.

Proof wins a late denial

When TRICARE denies a claim as late, what wins it back is proof the claim arrived inside the year: the 277CA from the payer, not just the 999 from your clearinghouse. TriWest reviews a late denial when you can show the claim was filed on time and it has a claim number.

The proof of timely filing guide covers what counts as proof, and the CO-29 guide covers how a timely filing denial shows up on a remittance.

text:
Severe flooding forced families out of their homes in McCaysville. Now, business owners are figuring out how to reopen, and police are working out of a bus.

In a Friday update, Police Chief Michael Otis Earley said the department lost "virtually everything," and city government buildings were severely damaged. Some businesses and government buildings had reopened just last week after earlier flooding, he said.

"We do not know how long this recovery will take, and we cannot promise that tomorrow will be easy," Earley said. "But I can promise that we will continue standing beside our citizens and doing everything within our power to help our community recover."

The Fannin County Emergency Management Agency said crews rescued 57 people overnight. An emergency shelter at the Fannin County Recreation Center, 370 Tom Boyd Road in Blue Ridge, is open to displaced residents who can reach it safely. The Red Cross is helping families there.

Where residents can get water and offer help

City Hall is closed until further notice, and routine city services are suspended, Earley said. Police are operating from a mobile command bus behind City Hall at 223 Blue Ridge Drive, where the city is also distributing water. Anyone who wants to volunteer or donate must check in with officials there.

Access to downtown remains limited to authorized residents, business owners and emergency personnel. A mandatory curfew remains in effect from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. in the restricted area.

Flood damage shuts down local pharmacy

McCaysville Drug Center said it will stay closed while staff assess the damage, clean up, and make a plan to reopen safely. The pharmacy acknowledged customers' concerns about getting their medications and said it would post updates as soon as it could.

text:
Summary#

The bill would require the Secretary of Defense to start a five-year pilot program offering services from qualifying midwives to eligible TRICARE beneficiaries. The program must begin within one year of enactment. The Secretary may establish a permanent program if the pilot is judged successful.

The Secretary must send Congress an implementation plan within 180 days of enactment and annual reports on costs, participants, care outcomes, satisfaction, access, and the program’s effectiveness. Reports must also include recommendations about changes, extension, or making the program permanent.

What it means for you#

If you are an eligible TRICARE beneficiary, you could receive care through the pilot from a midwife who meets the bill’s professional standards and applicable state credentialing rules. The bill does not specify where the pilot would operate or which services it would cover.

Expenses#

The bill does not specify the pilot’s total cost or funding. It requires annual reports to Congress on total program costs and costs per beneficiary who receives care.

Proponents' View#

No publicly available information.

No publicly available information.

text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (WHKY) – North Carolina will receive $503,460 as part of a $40 million multistate settlement with Ahold Delhaize over allegations involving prescription drug prices, Attorney General Jeff Jackson said. Ahold Delhaize owns several supermarkets including Food Lion, Giant, Hannaford, and Stop and Shop.

The settlement resolves allegations that the company’s supermarkets reported inflated prescriptions drug prices to Medicare Part D, Medicaid and TRICARE, causing these insurance companies to pay more than they should have, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

The department said the supermarkets offered discounted prices to these programs, but allegedly did not report those prices as their usual and customary prices when submitting claims.

The settlement follows a whistleblower lawsuit filed in federal court in Pennsylvania. The North Carolina Department of Justice worked with other state and federal agencies to investigate this case and negotiate the settlement.

text:
Most Tricare health plan costs for military and retiree households will go up between 3% and 4% in 2027, with some steeper increases of 9% to 12% in the monthly premiums of Tricare’s premium-based health plans.

The Military Health System announced new rates Nov. 5. Many Tricare Prime and Tricare Select users will see increases in their annual enrollment fees and deductibles, with additional rises in copayments for medical services. Some of the biggest increases in 2027 will be to the monthly premiums for Tricare Retired Reserve and, as in 2025 and 2026, Tricare Young Adult members.

Read Next: Everything You Need to Know About Tricare Open Enrollment

Tricare open enrollment season, when members may change their health insurance coverage for the upcoming year, runs from Nov. 9 to Dec. 8.

The current costs for the Tricare Dental Program will last through February 2026. Tricare announced that its pharmacy costs will stay the same from 2026 to 2027.

Tricare Groups

Costs depend on which Tricare "group" members belong to, determined by the date the service member first entered the military. Group A consists of those who entered service before Jan. 1, 2018, while Group B includes those who entered after that date.

Enrollment Fees

Active-duty families pay no annual enrollment fees for either Tricare Prime or Tricare Select. Retirees do, however, and those fees will go up in the coming year.

Group A retirees enrolled in Tricare Select will see their annual enrollment fee increase from $375 to $389 for a family and from $186.96 to $193.92 for an individual. Group A retirees using Tricare Prime will see the enrollment fee for a family plan increase from $765 to $793, while an individual's costs will go from $381.96 to $396 annually.

Retirees in Tricare Group B will see similar increases. The annual enrollment fee for the Prime family plan will rise from $927 to $960, while the individual plan will go from $462.96 to $480. Enrollment fees for Tricare Select will increase from $1,191 to $1,233.96 for a family and from $594.96 to $616.92 for an individual.

Deductibles

Annual deductibles — the amount those using Tricare Select must pay out of pocket before Tricare makes any payments — will also increase in 2027. Members using Tricare Prime don't pay deductibles.

Group A active-duty family members and retirees will see no changes to the deductible amount.

But a military member with the rank of E-4 or below in Group B will see their family deductible increase from $132 to $137, while families with sponsors E-5 and above in Group B will see their deductible rise from $397 to $411.

Individual military members in Group B will also see their deductibles rise in 2027, from $66 to $68 for E-4 and below, and from $198 to $205 for E-5 and above.

Copayments

Many copayments will also go up in the upcoming year. The cost of a primary care visit for active-duty Tricare Select users with a family in Group A will go from $28 to $30 in 2027, while the primary care copay for Group B family members will go from $19 to $20.

Retirees using Tricare Select will see a primary care visit go from $38 to $40 in Group A and from $33 to $34 in Group B. Those using Tricare Prime will pay $27 for a primary care visit, up from $26.

Premiums

The monthly premiums for Tricare’s premium-based plans have the steepest increases in 2027.

For reservists, the premiums for Tricare Reserve Select will go from $57.88 per month to $60.54 per month for an individual member and from $286.66 to $307.48 for a family, increases of 4.6% and 7.3% respectively.

Tricare Retired Reserve premiums will increase from $645.90 to $707.59 for an individual and from $1,548.30 to $1,697.7 for a family, increases of 9.6%.

Premiums for the Tricare Young Adult Program for members' dependents ages 21 to 26 will go from $794 a month to $893 for Prime coverage, a 12.5% increase following a 9.2% increase in 2026; and from $363 to $394 for Select, up 8.5%.

Catastrophic Cap

The catastrophic cap is Tricare beneficiaries' maximum out-of-pocket cost for all health care provided each year. It limits beneficiaries' liability in the case of a serious illness or injury. Once a beneficiary has hit the cap through copayments or pharmacy charges during the year, Tricare will pay the rest in full.

Group A retirees using Tricare Select will see this cap increase in 2027 from $4,381 to $4,538; and for retirees in Group B, it will go up from $4,635 to $4,802.

While the cap for active-duty family members in Group A who have either Tricare Select or Tricare Prime will remain the same at $1,000 annually, those in Group B will see it increase from $1,324 to $1,372.

title: How to spot a stolen valor scam this Veterans Day - KNSI
description:
What Is a Stolen Valor Scam?
A stolen valor scam involves someone either falsely claiming they served in the military or exaggerating their service.
A few high-profile stolen valor scams have made their way into mainstream consciousness.
Recognizing a Veteran-Targeted Scam Closely related to stolen valor scams are scams that prey specifically on veterans.
The Stolen Valor Romance Scam In most cases, stolen valor scams only affect public agencies like Veterans Affairs or government programs like TRICARE rather than individuals’ bank accounts.
text:
Keeping your identity and finances above board when scammers seem intent on defrauding anyone who answers the phone requires vigilance and caution. PeopleFinders shares information on the latest veteran-targeted scams.

What Is a Stolen Valor Scam?

A stolen valor scam involves someone either falsely claiming they served in the military or exaggerating their service. They often say that they served in combat when they saw no such action. Other times, they’ll lie about receiving decorations like the Medal of Honor, Purple Heart, Silver Star, or Bronze Star.

For stolen valor to become an actual scam, the fraudster has to actually collect benefits they haven’t actually earned. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2012 that stolen valor by itself is protected by the First Amendment and not a crime, though many (if not most) people find it highly objectionable.

A few high-profile stolen valor scams have made their way into mainstream consciousness. In 2017, the CNBC series “American Greed” featured Darryl Wright, an Idaho man who claimed he sustained wounds from enemy fire in Iraq.

No such thing happened, but Wright still collected around $750,000 in improper benefits (from more than a dozen public programs) before being convicted. He served two years in prison and was forced to pay $646,000 in restitution.

Recognizing a Veteran-Targeted Scam

Closely related to stolen valor scams are scams that prey specifically on veterans. They have a lot in common with general imposter and phishing scams that rely on stolen identities. Below are several types of scams veterans occasionally come across.

The “Veterans Savings Program” Scam

In August 2026, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued an alert about mailers going to veterans claiming they qualify for a new benefit under the VA. The postcards claim veterans can sign up for the “Veterans Savings Program,” but no such thing exists.

These mailers are just an old-fashioned phishing scam. The scammers count on recipients calling the phone number listed on the card and sharing sensitive information. From there, the scammers can apply for veterans’ benefits or sell the information on the dark web.

Overpayment Scam

Another veterans-directed scam involves fraudsters contacting veterans and informing them that the VA or some other public agency has given them too much money. To rectify the situation—and, according to scammers, avoid substantial criminal penalties—veterans must hand over some cash to their bank account.

PACT Act Scams

Signed into law by President Joe Biden in 2022, the PACT Act expanded benefits for millions of veterans exposed to toxic substances, including Agent Orange and burn pits. Veterans began receiving PACT Act benefits in 2024, and scammers have taken advantage of the attention the new program has received.

Fake Veterans’ Charities

Yet another military-adjacent scam that spikes during Veterans Day involves fake charities soliciting money on behalf of veterans. Scammers appeal to victims’ patriotic sensibilities with this scheme, which often employs cryptocurrency accounts and wire transfers.

TRICARE Scams

Many scammers target Medicare for illegitimate reimbursements, but others set their sights on TRICARE, the healthcare benefits program for former and active-duty military personnel (along with certain family members). Medicare and TRICARE get most of their funding from the federal government.

One common healthcare scam is known as phantom billing, which involves companies requesting reimbursement for products or services that patients never received. Sometimes, patients receive things their doctor never actually ordered. Both of these examples constitute healthcare fraud.

The Stolen Valor Romance Scam

In most cases, stolen valor scams only affect public agencies like Veterans Affairs or government programs like TRICARE rather than individuals’ bank accounts.

One exception lies with stolen valor romance scams. These schemes involve catfishers on dating websites falsely claiming that they’re deployed to a foreign country. That ruse gives them an excuse to skip out on video calls, send messages only intermittently, and otherwise conceal their identity.

Meanwhile, they constantly solicit money from their online matches. They pile on the lies by saying, for instance, that a family member has landed in the hospital. Romance scammers cast a wide net, and stolen valor is just one of the many tactics they use to convince victims to part with their money.

The Toll of Veterans-Directed Scams

The FTC estimated veterans, active-duty military personnel, and their families lost around $583 million in 2024. While the agency has not released 2025 figures yet, a comprehensive analysis completed by AARP suggests the number ballooned to $685 million last year.

Around 40% of veteran-directed fraud is owed to imposters. Imposter scammers often pose as representatives from government agencies or military banks, which lends credibility to their schemes. The U.S. as a whole lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025.

Responding to a Suspected Veteran-Directed Scammer

The most important thing to remember: Never give out sensitive information over the phone unless you are expecting a call from the VA or other legitimate organization. That includes your Social Security, driver’s license, and Veteran Health Identification Card numbers. Hang up if you get suspicious.

Other tips for preventing scams from reaching you include:

Calling back the organization that purportedly contacted you using their official phone number.

Verifying a charity’s status (and existence) at Charity Navigator.

Use a people search website to verify names, phone numbers, and addresses.

Periodically check your TRICARE claims page to ensure nobody is fraudulently using your identity for money.

Be careful about what you reveal about yourself online and through social media.

Don’t forget to report suspected fraudsters to the FTC and your state attorney general’s office.

Prioritize Awareness this Veterans Day

The chances of a scammer contacting you may be low, but they certainly aren’t zero. Knowing what you’re up against goes a long way in the defense against scams and fraud. When you get a suspicious call, email, or letter, erring on the side of caution will never fail you.

text:
Matt Clark sets a 90-day timeline for new DHA initiatives

Clark aims to cut projects that do not support readiness

The 2026 Healthcare Summit will explore AI, warfighter readiness and more

Matt Clark, assistant director for research, development and acquisition at the Defense Health Agency, has introduced the DELIVER Care framework to guide research, development, acquisition and contracting activities across the agency’s enterprise, DVIDS reported Tuesday.

Defense health leaders are placing greater emphasis on warfighter readiness and faster delivery of medical capabilities to the force. Government and industry leaders will gather at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3 to discuss AI governance, combat support and readiness, access to care and other federal health priorities. Register now to hear directly from senior leaders shaping the future of military and federal healthcare.

Clark, who was sworn in by DHA Director Navy Vice Adm. Darin K. Via in September, serves as the agency’s component acquisition executive and senior procurement executive.

How Will the DELIVER Care Framework Support Military Healthcare?

Clark said the DELIVER Care framework will strengthen DHA’s role as a combat support agency by aligning research, development, acquisition and contracting work with the mission and the DHA director’s four strategic priorities. DELIVER stands for decisive effects through excellence, lethality, integration, velocity, enterprise partnerships, and readiness and resilience.

Under the framework, his team will identify what the force needs and when, then direct qualified personnel and resources toward the agency’s top priorities.

“Through this alignment, we will deliver the capabilities at the speed of relevance,” Clark noted.

He added that teams will be measured on mission outcomes and speed rather than adherence to legacy paperwork processes.

“Everything we do is about delivering care,” Clark said.

What Is Clark’s 30-60-90-Day Transition Plan?

Clark will roll out the DELIVER Care framework through a 30-60-90-day transition plan.

In the first 30 days, he intends to meet DHA teams in person to identify obstacles, assess risks and understand which processes are working well.

“I want people to tell me what isn’t working, and how we can fix it,” he said.

During the second phase, Clark’s team will narrow those findings into a limited number of priorities tied to DHA’s strategic priorities and combat support mission, while setting clear goals and improving the decision-making process.

By the 90-day mark, the enterprise will launch targeted initiatives backed by leadership accountability, tracking progress through improved data, defined metrics and regular reviews.

“We want to show what works, what needs help, and where leaders should act,” Clark noted.

He added that the plan seeks to accelerate acquisition, strengthen portfolio oversight and improve collaboration with partners inside and outside government. The enterprise will also wind down low-value projects that delay delivery without advancing the mission. According to Clark, any capability, technology or service DHA develops that does not support readiness or resilience “doesn’t belong with us.”

Who Is Matt Clark?

Clark is a retired U.S. Army colonel and public health executive whose career spans defense, science and global health security, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before retiring from the Army in August, he commanded the SHAPE Healthcare Facility and the U.S. Army Health Clinic Brussels in Belgium.

He previously served as medical chief executive at the Joint Program Executive Office for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense, overseeing over $2.1 billion in medical countermeasure programs. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Clark led all seven vaccine teams under Operation Warp Speed and later directed COVID-19 international response operations at the White House.

He co-founded CerFlux, a startup developing AI-supported tools for oncology patients.

What Other Recent Moves Has DHA Made?

The framework comes as DHA leadership pushes for a more data-driven military health enterprise. Via has said that to achieve DHA’s North Star, the agency should be synchronized and data-driven to deliver decisive warfighter support. He pointed to the Joint Trauma System as a model for using operational experience and data to drive continuous improvement in military medicine. DHA plans to apply that approach by establishing a Joint Warfighter Health System covering mental health, traumatic brain injury and infectious disease.

In August, Via said the agency plans to accelerate its acquisition of commercial technologies that provide measurable outcomes. He added that DHA intends to place greater emphasis on outcomes rather than specific products when acquiring technology.

DHA is also seeking industry tools to sustain and modernize its Data Exchange Platform, a core conduit for clinical and operational data across the Military Health System. The agency’s Enterprise Intelligence and Data Solutions Program Management Office released the opportunity under DHA’s commercial solutions opening. DHA wants cloud-native, AI-ready upgrades for the system, which links military health data with the Department of Veterans Affairs and other partners.
